extracted.intended_audience: civil and mechanical engineers, architects, builders, and sanitary authorities (late-19th-century practitioners and informed readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical construction and sanitary guidelines for locomotives, tunnels, dams, canals, and dwelling houses — describing site selection, dimensions, materials, methods, and sanitary precautions for 19th-century engineering and architecture works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locomotive tractive force and adhesion
rubrics_metrics.description: The tractive force which the engine is capable of exerting amounts to (20.48² x 24) / 46 = 218.4 lb. for each pound of effective pressure per square inch on the pistons. ... it would require but a mean effective pressure of 102½ lb. per square inch on the pistons to exert a pull of 10 tons. Inasmuch, however, as the engine weighs 44 tons empty and 51 tons in working order, and as all this weight is available for adhesion, this great cylinder power can be utilized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design must match cylinder power to adhesive weight so that high cylinder pressures produce usable tractive force; present the tractive force calculation and check that locomotive weight provides corresponding adhesion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locomotive frame and general construction
rubrics_metrics.description: The frames are deep and heavy, being 1 3/8 in. thick, and they are stayed by a substantial box framing at the smokebox end, by a cast-iron footplate at the rear end, and by the intermediate plate stays shown. The axle box guides are all fitted with adjusting wedges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use deep, heavily stayed frames with proper stays at both ends; fit axle box guides with adjustment wedges to ensure secure alignment and long service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axle spacing and spring arrangement
rubrics_metrics.description: The axles are spaced at equal distances of 4 ft. 3.1 in. apart, the total wheel base being thus 12 ft. 9.3 in. In the case of the 1st, 2d, and 3d axles, the springs are arranged above the axle boxes in the ordinary way, those of the 2d and 3d axles being coupled by compensating beams. In the case of the trailing axle ... each trailing axle box receives its load through the horizontal arm of a strong bell-crank lever ... coupled to the adjoining end of a strong transverse spring ... This arrangement enables the spring for the trailing axle to be kept clear of the firebox, thus allowing the latter to extend the full width between the frames. The trailing wheels are fitted with a brake as shown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify equal axle spacing; use compensating beams for coupled springs; employ bell-crank lever and transverse spring arrangement to clear the firebox on trailing axles; include braking on trailing wheels where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valve motion and clearance of rotating parts
rubrics_metrics.description: The valve motion is of the Gooch or stationary link type, the radius rods being cranked to clear the leading axle, while the eccentric rods are bent to clear the second axle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose valve motion type and design radius/eccentric rods so they are cranked or bent to clear axles and other obstructions; illustrate with sectional views for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boiler working pressure and proportions
rubrics_metrics.description: The boiler, which is constructed for a working pressure of 147 lb. per square inch, is unusually large, the barrel being 60.4 in. in diameter inside the outside rings; it is composed of plates 0.65 in. thick.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify working pressure and dimension boiler barrel and plate thickness accordingly; ensure plate thickness and barrel diameter are sufficient for intended pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Firebox form and crown stays
rubrics_metrics.description: The firebox spreads considerably in width toward the top, ... The inside firebox is of copper and its crown is stayed directly to the crown of the casing by vertical stays, as shown, strong transverse stays extending across the boiler just above the firebox crown to resist the spreading action caused by the arrangement of the crown stays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design firebox to permit full width between frames when needed; use copper inner firebox and vertical crown stays with transverse stays above to resist spreading; flange back plates to enable rivetting after fitting where necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Firegrate dimensions and heating surface calculations
rubrics_metrics.description: The firegrate is 6 ft. 11.6 in. long by 3 ft. 4 in. wide. Heating surface: Tubes 1598.5 sq. ft; Firebox 102.5 sq. ft; total 1701.0 sq. ft. Firegrate area 23.3; Ratio of firegrate area to heating surface 1:73; Ratio of flue area through tubes to firegrate area 1:6.7; Ratio of least sectional area of chimney to firegrate area 1:17.26.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide detailed heating-surface and grate-area figures and check key ratios (grate to heating surface; flue area to grate; chimney area to grate) to achieve desired draught and steaming behaviour; note chimney proportions influence draught at slow speed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boiler tubes and dome/regulator arrangement
rubrics_metrics.description: The barrel contains 225 tubes 1.97 in. in diameter outside and 13 ft. 9½ in. long between tube plates. On the top of the barrel is a large dome containing the regulator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify tube count, diameter and length and provide dome containing regulator on barrel top for steam collection and control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exhaust and draught control for low-speed operation
rubrics_metrics.description: A grid is placed across the smokebox just above the tubes, and provision is made ... for closing the top of the exhaust nozzle, and opening a communication between the exhaust pipes and the external air when the engine is run reversed. The proportion of chimney area to grate is much smaller than in ordinary locomotives, this proportion having no doubt been fixed upon to enable a strong draught to be obtained with the engine running at a slow speed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include apparatus to vary exhaust paths (close/expose exhaust nozzle) for reverse running; use reduced chimney sectional area relative to grate to obtain stronger draught at low speeds when required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tunnel drainage and pumping provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Drainage headings ... will act as reservoirs into which the water from the main tunnel will be drained and run off to both sides of the Mersey, where gigantic pumps of great power and draught will bring the accumulating water to the surface ... The drainage shafts are sunk to a depth of 180 feet, and are below the lowest point of the tunnel, which is drained into them. Each drainage shaft is supplied with two pumping sets, consisting of four pumps, viz., two of 20 in. diameter, and two of 30 in. diameter. These pumps are capable of discharging from the Liverpool shafts 6,100 gallons per minute, and from the Birkenhead 5,040 gallons per minute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide drainage headings and shafts below the lowest tunnel invert; fit pumping sets sized to anticipated inflow rates with redundancy and contingency pumps to avoid delays from breakdowns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tunnel and heading dimensions and station sizing
rubrics_metrics.description: The heading is 7 feet in diameter ... The main tunnel, which is 26 feet wide and 21 feet high ... From the Liverpool side the tunnel now extends over 430 yards, and from the opposite shore about 590 yards. This includes the underground stations, each of which is 400 feet long, 51 feet wide, and 32 feet high.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define both heading and final tunnel dimensions (width, height) and station dimensions in plans; set out progress expectations and measure excavation against these baselines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tunnel lining, brickwork thickness and masonry proportions
rubrics_metrics.description: The tunnel is lined throughout with very solid brickwork, some of which is 18 inches thick (composed of two layers of blue and two of red brick), and toward the river this brickwork is increased to a thickness of six rings of bricks--three blue and three red. A layer of Portland cement of considerable thickness also gives increased stability to the brick lining and other portions of the tunnel, and the whole of the flooring will be bricked. There are about 22 yards of brickwork in every yard forward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify lining thickness appropriate to ground and water pressures; increase thickness in vulnerable sections; use Portland cement layers for stability; plan for heavy brickwork quantities per linear advance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tunnel safety niches, arch form and radii
rubrics_metrics.description: At every 45 ft. on alternate sides niches of 18 in. depth are placed for the safety of platelayers. The form of the tunnel is semicircular, the arch having a 13 ft. radius, the side walls a 25 ft. radius, and the base a 40 ft. radius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate safety niches at regular intervals; adopt an arch and wall radii appropriate to the tunnel profile to ensure shape stability and clearances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tunnel excavation methods and mechanization to increase speed
rubrics_metrics.description: In place of the miner's pick and shovel, which advanced at the rate of about ten yards per week, a machine known as the Beaumont boring machine will be brought into requisition ... it is expected to carry on the work at the rate of fifty yards per week. The work of excavation up to the present time has been done by blasting (tonite being employed for this purpose), and by the use of the pick and shovel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where feasible, substitute mechanical boring machines for manual excavation and blasting to multiply advance rates; plan for machine mobilization and account for differing rates in schedules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dam site selection and hydraulic design targets
rubrics_metrics.description: It was decided to locate the dam ... about the center of Carillon Rapid ... and to make it of a height sufficient to raise the reach between the head of Carillon and Chûte à Blondeau about six feet, and that above the latter two feet in ordinary water. At the site chosen the river is 1,800 feet wide, the bed is solid limestone, and more level or flat than is generally found in such places ... It was required to make it as near perfectly tight as possible and be, of course, always submerged. Allowing for water used by canal and slide and the leakage there should be a depth on the crest of the dam in low water of 2.50 feet and in high of about 10 feet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose sites with suitable bedrock and bank geology; determine crest heights and target upstream rises based on navigational objectives and hydrology; design dam to be tight and submerged with specified crest depths in low and high water.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporary works, timber sills and crib anchoring for dam construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Temporary structures ... were first placed immediately above the site of the dam to break the current. In shallow water timber sills 36 feet long and 12 inches by 12 inches were bolted to the lock up and down stream, having their tops a uniform height ... Each sill was fastened by five 1½ in. bolts driven into pine plugs forced into holes drilled from 18 inches to 24 inches into the rock. ... In the channels ... cribs 46 feet wide up and down stream were sunk ... The cribs were built ... of 12 in. X 12 in. timber ... They were fastened to the rock by 1½ in. bolts, five on each side of a crib ... The upstream side of the cribs were sheeted with 4 in. tamarack plank.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use temporary sills and cribs bolted to sound rock with specified bolt diameters and plug depths; sheet cribs on upstream side and clean rock bottoms by divers before installation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flat dam core construction, sheathing and stone filling
rubrics_metrics.description: On top of the 'platform' there was next built a flat dam of the sectional form shown ... It was built of 12 in. X 12 in. sawed pine timbers securely bolted ... and sheeted all over with tamarack 10 in. thick and the crest covered with ½ in. boiler plate 3 ft. wide. The whole structure was carefully filled with stone--field stone, or 'hard head' generally being used for the purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct permanent core of large timbers, sheath with thick tamarack planking, protect crest with steel/boiler plate and fill with durable stone to form a stable submerged dam face.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sluices, gates and method of closing openings
rubrics_metrics.description: At this stage ... The whole river--fortunately low--flowed through the sluices of which there were 113 ... Gates had been constructed with timber 10 in. thick, bolted together. They were hung on strong wooden hinges and, before being closed, laid back on the face of dam ... They were all closed in a short time ... To do this it was simply necessary to turn them over, when the strong current through the sluices carried them into their places ... The openings thus left were afterward filled up with timber and brushwood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide numerous sluices and robust timber gates hung on heavy hinges that can be turned into place using river current; plan methods to safely close and fill residual openings with timber and brush then stone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timber slide and bulkhead design for timber passage
rubrics_metrics.description: The timber slide was formed by binding parallel piers about 600 feet long up and down stream, ... and 28 ft. apart, with a timber bottom, the top of which at upper end is 3 ft. below the crest of dam. It has the necessary stop logs, with machinery to move them, to control the water. The approach is formed by detached piers, connected by guide booms, extending about half a mile up stream. Alongside of the south side of the slide a large bulkhead was built, 69 ft. wide, with a clear waterway of 60 ft. It was furnished with stop logs and machinery to handle them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design slides with parallel piers, adequate spacing, stop logs and handling machinery; provide guide booms for approach and large bulkheads with clear waterways and control logs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material quantities and cost accounting
rubrics_metrics.description: Table showing materials used in the dam and slide: Temporary works timber 134,500 cu. ft.; permanent dam timber 265,000 cu. ft.; slide timber 296,500 cu. ft.; iron lb. totals; stone filling cu. yds. etc. Total cost $332,000 (excluding surveys, engineering or superintendence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep detailed material take-offs and cost tables for temporary and permanent works and separate out surveys/engineering/superintendence as additional costs (approximately ten percent in this project).

rubrics_metrics.name: Canal embankment, puddle wall and riprap for ice protection
rubrics_metrics.description: The canal was formed by 'fencing in' a portion of the river-bed by an embankment built about a hundred feet out from the north shore ... On the canal side of it there is a wall of rubble masonry, laid in hydraulic cement, connecting the two locks, and backed by a puddle wall, three feet thick; next the river there is crib work from ten to twenty feet wide and the space between brick-work and puddle filled with earth. The outer slope is protected with riprap, composed of large bowlders. This had to be made very strong to prevent the destruction of the bank by the immense masses of moving ice in spring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct embankments with masonry walls backed by thick puddle walls and crib-work; protect outer slopes with heavy riprap sized to resist ice forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lock dimensions, wall thickness and gate/miter sill specification
rubrics_metrics.description: The locks are 200 ft. long in the clear between the gates, and 45 ft. wide in the chamber at the bottom. The walls of the lower one are 29 ft. high, and of the upper one 31 ft. They are from 10 to 12 ft thick at the bottom. The gates are 24 in. thick, made of solid timber ... The miter sills are made of 26 in. square oak.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify lock chamber length, width, wall heights and bottom thickness; design heavy timber gates and substantial oak miter sills similar to established canal practice (e.g., Lachine and Welland types).

rubrics_metrics.name: Canal construction sequencing and compaction
rubrics_metrics.description: In building the embankment the crib-work was first put in and followed by a part (in width) of the earth-bank. From that to the shore temporary cross-dams were built at convenient distances apart and the space pumped out by sections, when the necessary excavation was done, and the walls and embankments completed. The earth was put down in layers of not more than a foot deep at a time, so that the bank, when completed, was solid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct by sequence: install crib-work, place earth-bank in sections with temporary cross-dams, pump out sections to work dry; place fill in thin layers (≤1 ft) to ensure compaction and solidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dwelling site selection and subsoil treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: We must consider the localities in which they are to be situated, and the soil on which they are to rest. ... It is never safe to leave the top soil inclosed within the walls of our houses; and in many cases the subsoil should be covered with a layer of cement concrete, and at times with asphalt on the concrete. For if the subsoil be damp, moisture will rise; if it be porous, offensive matter may percolate through.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose healthy localities where possible; do not enclose topsoil within foundations; apply cement concrete (and asphalt where necessary) over subsoil to prevent rising damp and percolation of offensive matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cellar design and drainage avoidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Cellars are in many cases abominations. ... If cellars are necessary, they should be constructed with damp proof walls and floors; light should be freely admitted; every part must be well ventilated, and, above all, no drain of any description should be taken in. If they be constructed so that water cannot find its way through either walls or floors, where is the necessity of a drain?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid cellars when possible; if used, make cellars damp-proof, well-lit and ventilated, and avoid taking drains into them by designing floors/walls to keep water out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous damp course over internal and external walls
rubrics_metrics.description: The next important but oft neglected precaution is to have a good damp course over the whole of the walls, internal as well as external.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide damp-proof course continuously over all walls, including internal partitions, not just external walls, to prevent rising damp throughout the dwelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architectural and workmanship responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Architects and builders have much to contend with. ... Successfully to combat these opposing forces, two things are above all necessary, viz 1, a more perfect insight into the laws of nature, and a judicious use of serviceable appliances on the part of the architect; and, 2, greater knowledge, care, and trustworthiness on the part of workmen employed. ... Several cases have come under my notice, where, by reckless carelessness or dense ignorance on the part of workmen, dwellings which might have been sweet and comfortable if the architect's ideas and instructions had been carried out, were in course of time proved to be in an unsanitary condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Architects must apply sanitary knowledge and appropriate appliances and produce clear instructions; contractors and workmen must be competent and trustworthy to execute sanitary details exactly; inspect concealed works to ensure compliance.
